For demagnetizing fields < 900 Oe angular movements are often so small that mean directions cannot be plotted as distinct points on stereograms.

The corresponding poles have low latitudes. A similar effect was found by Faller & Soper (1979) using thermal demagnetization near the Curie point of magnetite. In the present case, these residual site mean directions formed a random set.

The dispersion of stable NRM directions is considerably less than the dispersion asso- ciated with the present geomagnetic field. Because of its high stability against alternating- field and thermal demagnetization the systematically directed NRM is considered to be thermoremanence, acquired when the rocks cooled through the Curie point of the principle magnetic minerals (magnetite). Isotopic age determinations suggest that this stable NRM originated between 520 and about 600 m.y.

The central unit, termed 'ana- tectic quartz-syenite' by Bloomfield, is not a simple igneous rock; it contains plagioclase and microperthite, quartz, biotite, amphibole, clino- pyroxene, an'd hypersthene with auxiliary apatite, zircon, calcite, and iron ore, which is almost certainly magnetite. Complex inter- growths of quartz and feldspar, and sometimes quartz and biotite, are seen in some specimens.

The mean direction of stable NRM was 311.3øE, +42.8 ø (downward), which corresponds on the geocentric dipole model to a palcomagnetic pole at 15.1øN, 27.8øW. At the other four sites either the stable component was too small relative to the IRM to be isolated from it by af demagnetization or it was not detected at all. The dispersion of stable NRM directions is considerably less than the dispersion asso- ciated with the present geomagnetic field.

The usefulness of the thermal treatments was (1) that. the bulk of the remanence was seen to have the char- acteristics of IRM, and (2) that the conver- gence of directions at the same seven sites was toward the same stable end direction, which had been derived from af measurements; this strongly supports the stability of the com- ponent in the direction D = 811.3, I = +42.8 ø .

The time of cooling through the Curie point is likely to have been closer to the time of intru- sion than to the time recorded by the K/Ar ages. Unfortunately, the presence of a large IRM component prevents the detection of a viscous PTRM [Chamalaun, 1964; Briden, 1965], which would be expected if the rocks were maintained for tens of millions of years at elevated temperatures below the Curie point.

Lightning currents may give rise to “hard” I.R.M. of relatively high coercivity (Cox 1961, Graham 1961). “Viscous” I.R.M. of low coercivity is believed to arise from the presence of either single or multi-domain grains of relaxation time less than the age of the rock (Irving, Stott &Ward 1961). An empirical approach is therefore necessary in choosing the appropriate demagnetizing field for specimens from a given site.

Two other cores showed anomalous directions of magnetiza- tion. Thin sections from these showed serpentinization and some secondary magnetite. A thin section from one of the seven cores first mentioned showed negligible alteration.

In thin section the rock was seen to be very fresh. No other pyroxenite site sampled gave a useful result, probably because of alteration with formation of secondary magnetite, visible in thin section. Directions of N.R.M. at this site have a significant mean on Watson’s criterion, although k is only I ‘7, because N is 26.

At one of these sites a thin section shows extensive alteration to serpentine with considerable secondary magnetite. At the other site a thin section shows traces of secondary magnetite. A third site in the Hartley Complex was located in norite at the Umsweswe River.
In the Selukwe Complex one site was located in harzburgite on the opposite side of the Dyke from Site 5. This harzburgite proved to be serpentinized with secondary magnetite.

Remanent magnetiza- tions of all specimens were measured using a cryogenic mag- netometer. A saturation magnetization (Js) versus tempera- ture (T) experiment was also conducted on a magnetic separate from 12 specimens of the Cachuma Formation to help identify the magnetic mineralogy of these clastic rocks (Figure 6). Components of magnetization isolated by thermal and af demagnetization were fitted with least squares lines [Kirsch- vink, 1980], and the site-mean and overall-mean directions (Tables 1 and 2) are plotted in Figures 7 and 8.

This metamorphism is dated at around 26.5 Ma by Nzien- gui (1993). Thus the NRM carried by extremely stable fine-grained, probably single domain, pyrrhotite (Rochette and Lamarche, 1986 and Ro- chette et al., 1990) with a Curie temperature between 310°C and 335°C (Fig. 2a), is probably a thermore- manent magnetization (TRM) acquired during post metamorphic cooling. The occurence of antipodal normal and reverse polarities as a function of the altitude especialy in area 1 and 2 (Table 1), supports this interpretation.

In order to test the occurrence of post metamorphic rotations or tiltings, a paleomagnetic study was undertaken in 44 sites from the inverted half graben of Bourg d'Oisans ("Zone Dauphinoise", Western Alps). The magnetization carried by pyrrhotite was acquired after metamorphic culmination, around the Oligo-Miocene limit. No obvious rotations around a vertical axis, are recorded.

Tak- ing into account the age constraints on metamor- phism and tectonic phases, we can propose an age for remanence acquisition. If NRM is a CRM, its age is the one of pyrrhotite formation during the meta- morphism which occured at around 26.5 Ma (Nziengui, 1993), that is late Oligocene. If NRM is in fact a TRM, it dates from the post-metamorphic cooling, so we can suggest it began at about the Oligo-Miocene time boundary.

Unimodal, near-symmetric distributions of feldspar ages within a volcaniclastic deposit suggest origi- nation from an eruptive event that rapidly saturated the depositional environment with juvenile pyroclastic material. Older, probably detrital feldspars are often present, however, and occasionally rival the youngest age com- ponent in abundance.

Specimens from the Malue Beds all exhibit relatively simple hysteresis loops which reach saturation by about 0.3 T (Figure 8), without any evidence of\"wasp-waisted\" behavior [Channell and McCabe, 1994], indicating that high-coercivity phases (e.g., hematite) are not present in significant proportions. The samples were pulse magnetized in 15 direct field steps up to 900 mT using a Sapphire Instruments SI-6 pulse magnetizer and then AF demagnetized in 10 steps up to 160 mT. All specimens reached 90 % of saturation between 60 and 150 mT, and then climbed slowly to 100 % at 900 mT, suggesting that their ChRM is carried by a mixture of single, pseudosingle, and multidomain magnetite. This interpretation is consistent with the results from AF demagnetization of the specimens’ SIRM, which show a rapid intensity decrease by 50 to 120 mT and then a slow decrease of the remaining few percentage of the SIRM intensity, and with the thermal step demagnetization tests described previously.

Both reversible and irreversible high-temperature (20–700◦C) thermomagnetic curves were obtained, most of them with a pro- nounced Hopkinson peak and a strong decay in susceptibility at around ∼580◦C (Fig. 5e and f). Low-temperature thermomagnetic curves show a susceptibility peak at around −150◦C denoting the Verwey transition. These characteristics are typical of low- Ti titanomagnetite grains (Dunlop and Ozdemir, 1997), which are the main magnetic carriers of ChRM direction in the studied rocks.

Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acquisition curves for all samples are very similar, giving saturation fields of less than 300–400 mT (Fig. 5c). These coercivities are typical of magnetite or titanomagnetite minerals. Narrow-waisted hysteresis curves were obtained for samples from all sites, giving coercivities between 4.3 mT and 24.9 mT, also typical of (titano)magnetite grains.

Some samples (FR4-F1, FR5-G1, FR85-B1, FR144-C3, and FR145-A1) show hornblende rims replacing augite, and occasionally myrmekite (samples FR1-B1 and FR4-F1). In pol- ished section, the preserved euhedral magnetite crystals (Fig. 6A and B) are interpreted as the carriers of the ChRM. Minor quantities of hematite and martite (Fig. 6C) are present and probably result from late magmatic oxidation, but do not contribute significantly as remanence carriers of the ChRM.

This is consistent with the stable ChRM directions disclosed by thermal and AF treatment. These characteristics are typical of low- Ti titanomagnetite grains (Dunlop and Ozdemir, 1997), which are the main magnetic carriers of ChRM direction in the studied rocks.

For the impact melts, two magnetic carriers are indicated by thermal demagnetization patterns, thermomagnetic curves, hysteresis and IRM acquisition curves (Fig.3). In thermal demagnetization (Fig.3) and susceptibility versus temperature curves (Fig. 3), magnetic sus- ceptibility typically decays steeply at about 580 ◦C (pure mag- netite) followed by a continuous decrease until 700 ◦C (haematite).

Accordingly, hysteresis loops are wasp-waisted (Fig. 3), typical of a mixture of two ferromagnetic phases with distinct coercivities (Tauxe et al. 1996). These two phases are also observed in IRM acquisition curves that show two saturation steps (Fig. 3), the ﬁrst at ﬁelds below 1000 mT and the second at ﬁelds as high as 2500 mT . The AF demagnetization up to 140 mT effectively removed up to 80 per cent of the remanence for most samples.

The Characteristic Remanence Magnetization (ChRM) direction is recovered above demagnetization temperatures of 300° and persists up to 630 °C ( Fig. 2A–F). There is no apparent difference between directions recovered above and below 570 °C, suggesting that this remanence was acquired by both haematite and titanomagnetite at, or shortly after, the time of deposition. Furthermore, there is no apparent tendency for the polarity to change with changes in lithology, which is particularly important given the relatively high permeability of the sandstones and conglomerates in comparison to the paleosols and mudstones.

Microscopic Characteristics of the Magnetic Minerals Representative petrographic thin sections reveal that metallic minerals are black and opaque in plane and cross‐ polarized lights, while they appear light gray or off‐white in reflected light. Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) observations reveal that the metallic minerals range in size from 10 to 30 μm and are irregular in shape. They do not have oxidized edges, do not exist in cracks, and have a concave‐convex contact relationship with peripheral non‐metallic minerals (quartz, feldspar, etc.), which indicates that the magnetic carriers have not been remag- netized.

Moreover, the elements that make up the metallic minerals are mainly iron and oxygen, and the semi‐ quantitative Fe /O atomic ratio is mostly 2/3, suggesting that the metallic minerals may be hematite (Figures S6–S8 in Supporting Information S1 ).

The small amount of titanium may be an isomorph of hematite. Therefore, the magnetic carrier is detrital hematite, consistent with the unblocking temperature results and the decay curves of the detrital remanent magnetization intensity revealed by progressive thermal demagnetization in the next subsection. 3.3.

Following a viscous component's isolation (define the interval of 30–200°C), a Characteristic Remanent Magnetization (ChRM) component was isolated in 696 samples, which were used for magneto- stratigraphic considerations and the remaining 73 samples for the fold test (Figure 2 ). The remanent magnetic mineral is mainly composed of detrital hematite, according to microscopic observations and progressive thermal demagnetization results (Figures S4–S9 in Supporting Information S1 ). The direction of the Low Temperature Component (LTC) in situ coordinates is close to the current geomagnetic field (Declination = 0.5°, Inclina- tion = 50.3°, Figure S10 in Supporting Information S1 ).
